passages.happening:
Jesus goes back to Capernaum. A centurion there has a servant he values highly, and the servant is sick and close to death.

The centurion hears about Jesus and sends some Jewish elders to ask him to come and heal the servant. They plead with Jesus: “This man is worthy to have You grant this, for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue” (verses 4-5).

Jesus goes with them. But when he is near the house, the centurion sends friends with a message: “Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof” (verse 6). Just say the word, he says, and my servant will be healed. He knows how authority works: he gives orders, and they are done.

Jesus is amazed at him. He turns to the crowd and says, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith” (verse 9). The messengers go back and find the servant well.
passages.hearers:
Matthew tells this story too (Matthew 8:5-13), and its notes explain what a centurion was: an officer over a company of soldiers, in theory a hundred men. Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas under Rome, and many scholars think this officer most likely served in Antipas's forces, organized in the Roman way. Either way he was a Gentile, a non-Jew.

Luke tells it differently. In Matthew the centurion speaks to Jesus himself. In Luke he never meets Jesus at all. He sends Jewish elders first, and then friends. Some readers think Matthew tells the story in short form, counting the messengers' words as the centurion's own, the way we say a ruler ‘said’ what his messengers said. Others think Luke kept the fuller telling. Both views are held.

Only Luke has the elders' words. This Gentile loves the Jewish people and has paid for their synagogue. In Acts Luke tells of other Gentiles like him, who honoured Israel's God without becoming Jews. The centurion Cornelius was “devout and God-fearing” and “gave generously to the people” (Acts 10:2).

Notice the two sides of the man. The elders say he is ‘worthy’. He says he is ‘not worthy’. The humble man is the one Jesus praises.

In Luke's Greek the sick man is called a slave. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. Luke notes that this one was ‘highly valued’, dear to his master.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, outsiders who trusted Israel's God are honoured. Naaman the Syrian, whom Jesus named at Nazareth (4:27), was healed and confessed, “there is no God in all the earth except in Israel” (2 Kings 5:15). Ruth the Moabite came to trust in Israel's God and became an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:17).

The centurion trusts that a word is enough. The psalm says of God, “He sent forth His word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20).
passages.hard: Is Jesus saying Gentiles have more faith than Jews? No. The elders who bring the request are Jews who care for this man and believe Jesus can help. Jesus is a Jew speaking to Jews. His point is that great faith turned up where many would not expect it, in a soldier of the occupying power. It is a warning against assuming that faith belongs to the insiders and a promise that the door is open to outsiders. It is not a verdict on Israel.
passages.asks: The centurion was a man of power who knew he had no claim on Jesus. Yet he was also a man who cared for a slave. What would it look like to come to God the way he did, with no sense that you deserve anything, and with full trust that a word from Jesus is enough?

passages.t: A widow's only son, at the gate of Nain
passages.happening:
Soon afterward Jesus goes to a town called Nain. His disciples and a large crowd go with him.

As he comes near the town gate, a funeral is coming out. The dead man is “the only son of his mother, and she was a widow” (verse 12). A large crowd from the town is with her.

When the Lord sees her, his heart goes out to her. “Do not weep,” he says (verse 13). He goes up and touches the coffin, and the bearers stand still. “Young man,” he says, “I tell you, get up!” (verse 14). The dead man sits up and begins to speak, and Jesus gives him back to his mother.

Awe falls on everyone. They praise God and say, “A great prophet has appeared among us!” and “God has visited His people!” (verse 16). The news spreads through Judea and all the region.
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story. Nain was a village in Galilee, usually identified with the modern village of Nein on the slope of the hill of Moreh, a few miles from Nazareth.

Think of what this woman had lost. Her husband had already died. Now her only son was dead. In that world a widow with no son could be left with no one to provide for her or speak up for her. Luke says nothing about what she said or did. She did not ask Jesus for anything. Jesus saw her and came to her.

‘His heart goes out to her’ translates a strong Greek word for being moved deep inside. It is a feeling in the gut, not a polite pity.

Burial came quickly. In Acts, Ananias and Sapphira are buried within hours of dying (Acts 5:6-10). The body was carried out of town to be buried. This was probably an open bier, since the young man sits up. Touching a dead body, or what carried it, made a person unclean under the law (Numbers 19:11). Jesus touches it anyway. Instead of death making him unclean, his life reaches the dead.

Luke, telling the story, calls Jesus ‘the Lord’ here, a title he will use of him again and again. The one who stops the funeral is the Lord of life.
passages.ot:
The crowd says ‘a great prophet’ because they know their Scriptures. Elijah raised a widow's son at Zarephath, and then he “gave him to his mother” (1 Kings 17:23). Luke uses the same words: Jesus “gave him back to his mother” (verse 15). Elisha raised a woman's son at Shunem (2 Kings 4:32-37). Shunem lay on the other side of the same hill from Nain, only a few miles away.

The law and the psalms say again and again that God himself looks after widows. God is “a defender of the widows” (Psalm 68:5). He “executes justice for the fatherless and widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18). ‘God has visited His people’ is what Zechariah sang at the start of the book (1:68).
passages.hard:
If you have lost someone and no miracle came, this story does not say you were loved less than the widow of Nain. Her son was given back for a while, and in time he would die again. Jesus did not empty every grave in Galilee. What the story shows is who Jesus is: the Lord who sees the grieving, comes near to them, and is stronger than death. The promise he makes to all who trust him is the resurrection at the last day. “I am the resurrection and the life,” he tells another grieving woman (John 11:25).

Jesus said ‘Do not weep’ just before he raised her son. It is not a rule against crying at funerals. Elsewhere Jesus himself wept at a friend's grave (John 11:35). Grief is not unbelief. If grief is crushing you, do not carry it alone. Reach out to people you trust, to a pastor, or to someone trained to help.
passages.asks: The widow did not ask for anything. Jesus saw her, and his heart went out to her. If you are grieving, he sees you too, and he does not stand at a distance. And who around you is grieving alone, whom you could see and come near to?

passages.happening:
John's disciples tell him about all these things. John, who is in prison, sends two of them to ask the Lord, “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” (verse 19).

At that very hour Jesus heals many people of diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and gives sight to many who are blind. Then he answers: “Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor” (verse 22). And he adds, “Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Matthew tells this too (Matthew 11:2-6), and its notes explain it more fully. John had preached that one more powerful was coming, with a winnowing fork and fire (3:16-17). What he heard about was healing, teaching and meals with tax collectors. And John was still in Herod's prison (3:20).

Only Luke says that Jesus healed many ‘at that very hour’. John's messengers did not take back a rumour. They saw it with their own eyes.

The list in verse 22 is almost the Nazareth reading again (4:18), with more added. Luke has just told of a leper cleansed (5:12-16) and a dead man raised (7:11-17).

A broken scroll found in a cave by the Dead Sea, known as 4Q521, speaks of a coming day when the Lord will heal the wounded, give life to the dead and bring good news to the poor. It shows that some Jews of the time linked these very works with the age of God's anointed one. John's disciples would have understood.
passages.ot: Jesus' answer is woven from Isaiah: “the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5); “Your dead will live” (Isaiah 26:19); and good news preached to the poor (Isaiah 61:1). He does not say ‘Yes, I am’. He points to the works the prophets promised and lets John draw the line himself.
passages.hard:
Did John doubt? He had baptized Jesus and heard the voice from heaven. Christians have read it two ways. Some think John did not doubt, but sent his disciples so they would see Jesus for themselves. Many think the question was real. John had pictured the coming one bringing judgment, and what he heard did not fit. A prison cell is also a dark place to think in. Both readings are held.

What is plain is how Jesus treats the question. He does not scold John. He sends him evidence and a gentle blessing. Then he praises John in front of the crowd. Doubt in a faithful person is not the same as unbelief. If the darkness in you is heavy and does not lift, please talk to someone who can help: a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line.
passages.asks: John took his question to Jesus. Do you have a question about Jesus that you are afraid to ask? Bring it to him, and look at what he has done. ‘Blessed is the one who does not fall away’ is a promise, not a threat, for anyone who is tempted to give up because Jesus is not doing what they expected.

passages.t: More than a prophet; children in the market
passages.happening:
When John's messengers leave, Jesus speaks to the crowds about John. What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed blowing in the wind? A man in fine clothes? Those are in palaces. A prophet? “Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (verse 26). John is the messenger the Scriptures promised. “I tell you, among those born of women there is no one greater than John, yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he” (verse 28).

All the people who hear this, even the tax collectors, agree that God is right, because they had been baptized by John. But the Pharisees and experts in the law reject God's purpose for themselves, because they had refused John's baptism.

Then Jesus says the people of this generation are like children sitting in the market, calling to each other: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a funeral song, and you did not weep.’ John came fasting, and they said he had a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they called him a glutton and a drunkard, “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (verse 34). “But wisdom is vindicated by all her children” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Matthew tells most of this too (Matthew 11:7-19), and its notes explain the reed, the fine clothes and the children's game. Crowds had walked out to the Jordan to hear John. A reed bends whichever way the wind blows. John did not. He was in prison for telling a ruler the truth.

Verses 29 and 30 are found only in Luke. They show the split in the crowd. The tax collectors, who were despised, had gone to John and turned to God. Some of the most religious people had not. Luke's word ‘rejected God's purpose for themselves’ is sad. They turned down what God had planned for their good.

Children in a town square played at grown-up life: a wedding with a pipe and dancing, a funeral with sad songs. Some children would not join any game. John was too strict for people; Jesus was too free. The complaints point in opposite directions. The real problem was that people did not want to hear either of them.

‘Vindicated’ means proved right. Matthew says wisdom is proved right ‘by her actions’ (Matthew 11:19). Luke says ‘by all her children’: the people who actually listen and turn, like the tax collectors of verse 29.
passages.ot:
The verse Jesus quotes about John is from Malachi: “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me” (Malachi 3:1). In Malachi, the messenger prepares the way for the Lord himself. Jesus applies the promise to John, and so to himself as the one who comes after.

In Proverbs, wisdom is pictured as a woman who calls out in the streets and invites people to her table (Proverbs 9:1-6). Her ‘children’ are those who accept the invitation.
passages.hard:
How can the least in the kingdom be greater than John? It does not mean John is shut out. It means John stood at the edge of something new. He pointed to Jesus but died before the cross and the empty tomb. The humblest follower who has seen those things stands in a better place than even John did.

‘A glutton and a drunkard’ was an insult. Jesus repeats it so that people can see what they were doing. He did eat with sinners. He did not live as a drunkard.
passages.asks: It is easy to find a reason not to listen to God's messengers: too strict, too free, too serious, too relaxed. What excuse do you use? The tax collectors had more to lose and listened anyway. Which group in this story are you in?

passages.happening:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to eat with him, and Jesus goes in and reclines at the table. A woman of the town, known as a sinner, hears that he is there. She brings an alabaster jar of perfume.

She stands behind him at his feet, weeping. Her tears wet his feet, and she wipes them with her hair. She kisses his feet and pours perfume on them.

The Pharisee, whose name is Simon, thinks to himself that if Jesus were a prophet he would know what kind of woman is touching him. Jesus answers his thought with a story. Two men owed money to a lender, one five hundred denarii and the other fifty. Neither could pay, so he forgave them both. “Which one, then, will love him more?” (verse 42). Simon answers, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more” (verse 43).

Jesus turns to the woman and says to Simon, “Do you see this woman?” (verse 44). You gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with tears. You gave me no kiss; she has not stopped kissing my feet. You did not put oil on my head; she has poured perfume on my feet. “Therefore I tell you, because her many sins have been forgiven, she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little” (verse 47).

He says to her, “Your sins are forgiven” (verse 48). The other guests begin to ask who this is who even forgives sins. Jesus says to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (verse 50).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story. At a formal meal, guests lay on couches or cushions around the table, leaning on one elbow, with their feet stretched out behind them. That is how the woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet. Luke does not say how she got in, only that she came.

A denarius was about a day's pay for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). So one man owed more than a year's wages, the other about two months'. Neither could pay.

Washing a guest's dusty feet, a kiss of greeting, and oil for the head were marks of welcome (Genesis 18:4; Psalm 23:5). Simon gave none of them. They may not have been required, but Jesus noticed. The woman gave all three, and more: tears for water, kisses on his feet instead of his cheek, costly perfume instead of plain oil.

Letting down her hair in front of men would probably have shocked the guests. Much later, the Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, counted a wife going out with her head uncovered as grounds for divorce. That rule is later and may not show how things were in a Galilean town, but it suggests how the gesture might have looked.

Who was she? Luke does not name her. She is not Mary Magdalene, whom Luke introduces as someone new in the very next chapter (8:2). She is not Mary of Bethany, Lazarus's sister, who anoints Jesus' feet in John's Gospel, at a different time and place, just before his death (John 12:1-8). In the West, from a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great in 591, the three women were often blended into one, and she was preached as a reformed sinner. The Eastern churches always kept them apart. The Gospels themselves never join them.

What was her sin? Luke calls her ‘a sinful woman’ and Simon calls her ‘a sinner’, but neither says what she had done. Many sermons and paintings have made her a prostitute. The text does not say so, and these notes do not guess.

Simon is not a villain. He invited Jesus and called him ‘Teacher’. He thought a true prophet would know who was touching him and keep away. Jesus did know who she was. That is why he let her stay.
passages.ot:
The Psalms speak of the joy of being forgiven: “Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1). God's invitation in Isaiah is for people whose sins seem too deep to wash out: “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18).

‘Go in peace’ is an old blessing. Eli the priest sent away Hannah, who had been weeping before God, with the words “Go in peace” (1 Samuel 1:17).
passages.hard:
Which comes first, her love or her forgiveness? Verse 47 can be read two ways, and the Greek allows both.

Many readers take her love as the evidence that she had already been forgiven. The story Jesus tells points that way: the one forgiven more loves more. The end of the verse points the same way: he who is forgiven little loves little. On this reading, the woman had already met Jesus' forgiveness, perhaps when she heard him speak, and her tears are thanks.

Others, from early centuries, have read her love as part of the way she came to forgiveness: she came to Jesus in love and sorrow, and that love and repentance were met with pardon. Many hold the two together, and point to the last words: “Your faith has saved you” (verse 50). Love and forgiveness meet in her trust in Jesus. Christians have read the verse in all these ways, and these notes take no side. Every reading agrees that Jesus forgave her fully and sent her away in peace.

Many readers have assumed that her sin was sexual, though Luke does not say. If you carry shame about something sexual, this story is for you. Jesus let her come close when the room wanted her gone, and he spoke of her with honour. If what happened to you was not your choice, it is not your sin, and you deserve safety and help from someone you trust.
passages.asks: Jesus asked Simon, ‘Do you see this woman?’ Simon saw a sinner. Jesus saw a person who loved much. When you look at someone with a past, what do you see? And if you are the one with the past, hear what Jesus said to her: your sins are forgiven; your faith has saved you; go in peace.
